lines.v: Most of us have seen the determinant in school.
For a two-by-two matrix, it's a d minus b c.
For a three-by-three, it looks like this.
There are many ways to write it.
Expand along a row,
multiply the eigenvalues,
or add up signed products.
And it shows up all over mathematics.
It decides whether a system of linear equations has a unique solution.
It measures how much a linear transformation scales space.
And it even finds the area of any polygon.

For a computer scientist, one of the most important things about the determinant is that it's fast to compute: Gaussian elimination does it in about n cubed steps, and even faster if you really want to.
There's even a whole field, algebraic complexity theory, that asks how efficiently polynomials can be computed. There, the determinant is the model of an easy polynomial.
Its twin, the permanent, is the same sum without the minus signs. And it is believed to be much harder.

In 1979, Leslie Valiant showed that computing the permanent is sharp-P complete: as hard as counting the solutions of any problem in NP. An efficient algorithm for it would mean P equals NP, and much more.
So counting is usually hard. And yet, determinants, with their minus signs, are one of the rare tricks that can count efficiently. One of the most beautiful places I've found this is combinatorics.
And today, I want to share that with you: how determinants can count.
Let's start with a simple puzzle.
Meet these two ants.
They both live in a grid-like world.
And they both want to get back home, right now.
On this grid, there are rules.
An ant can step up,
or step right.
But never left,
and never down.
Of course, there are many paths home. The blue ant could go this way, or this way. And the orange ant, this way, or that way.
But today, they can't just take any path. They had a fight, and if they meet, they'll start fighting again.
So neither will set foot on any dot the other one walks on. Not even later: ants leave a scent trail.
So here's the question: in how many ways can both ants get home, without ever meeting?
You can always find one easily. Here, the blue one goes up and around, and the orange one goes right and around. They never meet.
And here's one where they cross.
Let's check them all, one by one.
This pair works.
This one doesn't.
This one does.
And this one doesn't.
And so on.
Twenty pairs never meet, and sixteen do.
I know what you're thinking: this is stupid. There must be an easier way. Well, here comes an old friend.
Consider this two-by-two matrix, A. Its rows are the ants, and its columns are the houses.
The first entry counts the paths from the blue ant to its own home. There are six.
The second entry is a little sneakier: the paths from the blue ant to the orange ant's house. There are four.
And by symmetry, the orange ant gives the same numbers the other way round: four, and six.
By the way, counting paths on a grid is easy.
From the blue ant to its house, every path takes two steps right and two steps up, just in a different order.
So a path is just a choice of which two of the four steps go right: four choose two, which is six.
To the orange house, it's three steps right and one up. Four choose one: four.
Now find the determinant of A: six times six, minus four times four,
which is twenty. Voilà!
The same number as before.
In fact, there's nothing special about this scenario.
Take a bigger grid,
and bring in a few more ants, with homes of their own.
Now move the ants and their homes anywhere you like.
Build the same kind of matrix: each entry counts the paths from one ant to one house.
Its determinant is two hundred fifty-two.
And that's exactly the number of ways all four ants can get home, without any two of them ever meeting.
Isn't this so simple, and beautiful?
And I think, in understanding why this works lies the essence of how determinants can be used in counting problems.
So, let's get into that.
Why does this work?
Let's get back to our two ants.
Here's their matrix, and its determinant: six times six, minus four times four.
Why six times six? The blue ant has six ways home, and the orange ant has six.
Any blue path can go with any orange path, so six times six counts every pair of paths home: thirty-six.
Twenty of them never meet. Sixteen meet.

And four times four? The blue ant has four ways to the orange house, and the orange ant has four ways to the blue house. So four times four counts the pairs where the ants end up in the wrong houses: sixteen.
So the determinant is all the pairs, minus the wrong-house pairs.
But the pairs that never meet are all the pairs, minus the ones that meet.
So the determinant counts the pairs that never meet exactly when there are as many meeting pairs as wrong-house pairs. And there are: sixteen and sixteen.
But why is that?
Take a pair where the ants end up in the wrong houses.
The blue ant starts to the left of the orange one, and ends to its right.
So somewhere, they must share a dot.
Take the first shared dot, and swap the tails from there.
Now each ant is at its own home, and their paths meet.
Now the other way: a pair that meets on the way home.
Swap the tails at the first shared dot, and they end up in each other's houses.
Swap again at the same dot, and we're back where we started.
So for every pair of paths that meet, there's a matching pair where the ants go to the wrong houses. And the other way round.
This pair, that meets, goes with this one.
This one, with this one.
And this one, with this one.
And so on.
So there's a one-to-one match: the pairs that meet, and the wrong-house pairs, are exactly as many.
So now, the formula falls into place.
The determinant is all the pairs, minus the wrong-house pairs,
which is all the pairs, minus the ones that meet,
which is exactly the pairs that never meet.
Twenty.
A bijective proof: the only kind a combinatorialist fully trusts.
And with three ants? The same idea works, just with more terms.
The three-by-three determinant has six terms, one for each way of sending the ants to the houses: everyone home, two ants in each other's houses, or all three going round in a circle.
Each term counts the families of paths for that way, with a plus or a minus sign. Add them up, and you get fifty.
Now take a family where some ants meet. Find the first meeting, and swap the two ants' tails from there.
Two ants have traded houses, so the family moves to a term with the opposite sign. Swap again, and it comes back. So the two cancel.
Every family with a meeting has a partner like this. Watch them cancel.
All that's left are the families where nobody meets. And with the ants placed like this, they can only all go home: fifty of them. Exactly the determinant.
So far, ants on a grid. Now, the general lemma.
Here's how one famous book begins its chapter on this lemma.
The essence of mathematics is proving theorems, and so, that is what mathematicians do: they prove theorems.
But to tell the truth, what they really want to prove, once in their lifetime, is a Lemma.
That's from Proofs from THE BOOK, by Martin Aigner and Günter Ziegler.

The title comes from Paul Erdős, who liked to imagine that God keeps a book with the most beautiful proof of every theorem. You don't have to believe in God, he said, but you should believe in The Book.
And this is one of those lemmas.
It's called the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma. Bernt Lindström found it in 1973, and Ira Gessel and Xavier Viennot rediscovered it in 1985.
First, take a directed acyclic graph: dots joined by one-way arrows. Here, every arrow points to the right, so you can never come back to where you started.
Now pick any starting points on the left, a one up to a n, and the same number of ends on the right, b one up to b n.

But keep the ends in the same order as the starts: first to first, second to second, like lanes. Then if the destinations get mixed up, say a two going to b three and a three going to b two, the paths are forced to cross.
Build a matrix M: the entry in row i, column j is the number of paths from a i to b j. For example, from a one to b two.
Then the determinant of M counts the families of paths, a one to b one, all the way to a n to b n, that never touch.
So any puzzle that is secretly a family of paths that never touch, a determinant can count.
Does the pattern repeat? Let's look.
Take a hexagon, cut into little triangles.
Glue two neighbours together and you get a tile. Tiles point in three directions.
Now cover the hexagon with tiles: no gaps, no overlaps. Notice anything? It looks like a stack of boxes.
It's completely flat. Your brain is doing the 3D for free.
How many ways can you tile it?
Fade out the flat tiles. The others link up into chains, from left to right.
Tiles never overlap, so the chains never touch.
Now squash the hexagon onto our grid, and the two chains become our two ants.
So there are twenty tilings. All this time, our ants were tiling a hexagon.
Make the box bigger: three by three by three, and stack the boxes in.
Now there are three chains, so three ants.
Squash it onto a grid: three ants that never touch.
Same recipe as before: count the paths from each ant to each house, and take the determinant.
Nine hundred and eighty stacks of boxes.
Percy MacMahon counted these over a century ago, with heavy algebra. Our ants do it with one determinant.
Here's a mountain range: every step goes up or down, and it never dips below sea level. It starts and ends at sea level.
How many ranges are there? With two steps, just one. With four steps, two. Six steps: five. Eight steps: fourteen.
One, two, five, fourteen: these are the Catalan numbers, one of the most famous sequences in combinatorics.
They count many things. Read each up-step as an opening bracket, and each down-step as a closing one: every range becomes a balanced string of brackets.
They also count the ways to cut a pentagon into triangles: five again.
Now draw two ranges, one inside the other, and they must never touch.
They're paths again: two walkers, starting here and here, ending here and here.
From the blue start to the blue end is four steps: two ranges. To the orange end, six steps: five. The orange walker gets five, and fourteen.
So the matrix is made of Catalan numbers, and its determinant, two times fourteen minus five times five, is three.
And here they are: exactly three.
And one more, a real beauty: the Aztec diamond. Rows of two, four, six squares, and then back down.
Cover it with dominoes. Each domino covers two neighbouring squares.
The smallest diamond can be tiled in two ways.
The next one, in eight ways.
The next, in sixty-four.
Guess the next one.
One thousand and twenty-four. Powers of two, every single time. That's suspicious.
Here's the trick. Colour the board like a chessboard.
Now every domino is one of four kinds: lying flat or standing up, and starting on a light or a dark square.
Give each kind a job: a flat step, a step up, a step down, or nothing at all.
Put the steps together, and they link up into paths, from the left side to the right side.
Dominoes never overlap, so the paths never touch. And every pair of paths that never touch comes from exactly one tiling.
So, same recipe as before: count the paths from each start to each end.
Two times six, minus two times two: eight. Exactly the eight tilings.
One size up, there are three paths, and a three-by-three determinant gives sixty-four.
In general, the diamond of order n has two to the power n times n plus one over two tilings. A determinant, hiding in a pile of dominoes.
Now pick one tiling at random, every tiling equally likely, on a big diamond, and let it grow.
This is order sixty.
The corners freeze into brick walls. The middle is chaos. And as the diamond grows, the boundary between them becomes a perfect circle.
It's called the arctic circle theorem.

data.title: Card: When the signs go wrong

lines.v: But not every counting problem is secretly paths. What then?
With the ants, the bad terms cancelled on their own: every pair that met had a swapped partner with the opposite sign.
With dominoes, nothing like that happens by itself. So we'll have to fix the signs ourselves.
Take dominoes on a chessboard. Dominoes aren't paths, but there's a determinant trick here too. Start small: a two-by-three board.
It can be tiled in exactly three ways: three standing dominoes; one standing on the left and two lying flat; or two lying flat and one standing on the right.
Notice: a domino always covers one dark square and one light square, right next to each other.
So build a matrix: one row for each dark square, and one column for each light square.
Put a one wherever a dark and a light square touch, and a zero where they don't.
Now, a three-by-three determinant is a sum of six terms. Each term picks one entry from every row and every column, and multiplies them.
Let's go through all six.
Three of the six terms pick up a zero, so they vanish.
The other three pick only ones. And each of them is exactly a tiling: a picked one is a dark and a light square that touch, which is a domino.
So the determinant should be three. It's minus one.
The culprit is the signs. Each term also gets a sign: plus if its pattern can be sorted with an even number of swaps, minus if it takes an odd number.
This tiling needs two swaps, so it gets a plus. These two need one swap each, so they get a minus.
One, minus one, minus one: minus one. The cancellation eats the good ones.
In 1961, the physicist Pieter Kasteleyn had an idea: if the signs don't cancel the way you want, change the signs.
Draw the board as a graph: a dot for each square, and an edge for each pair of squares that touch. Every edge is a place a domino could go.
Now put a minus sign on just this one edge. In the matrix, its one becomes a minus one.
Which tilings notice? Only the ones that use this edge, and only the all-standing tiling does.
Its term was plus one. Now one of its three entries is minus one, so the term becomes minus one. The other two terms never use that edge, so they stay the same.
Now every tiling carries the same sign, so nothing can cancel. The determinant is minus one, minus one, minus one: minus three.
Ignore the sign, and you get three: exactly the number of tilings.
Let's try a bigger board: four by four. It has thirty-six tilings.
Build the plain matrix, eight by eight, and take its determinant. It says there are zero tilings. Very confident, very wrong.
Here's what happened: eighteen tilings come with a plus sign, and eighteen with a minus. They cancel perfectly.
So use Kasteleyn's trick: put minus signs on the vertical edges of every other column.
Now all thirty-six tilings get the same sign, and the determinant gives thirty-six. Exactly right.
Why does every other column work? Look at any little square of four edges. It always has exactly one minus sign: an odd number.
That's Kasteleyn's rule: if every little square has an odd number of minus signs, then every tiling gets the same sign. Let's see why.
Take two tilings, and lay one on top of the other.
Where they agree, nothing happens. Where they differ, their dominoes join up into closed loops. Here, there are two.
To go from one tiling to the other, you turn each loop: every domino on it slides over by one.
The small loop first. Two flat dominoes become two standing ones. That's one swap, so the sign flips once.
But the standing pair uses exactly one minus edge, so it flips once more. Two flips: no change.
Now the big loop. Turning it takes three swaps: three flips. And it picks up one minus edge: a fourth flip. Again, no change.
Kasteleyn showed that this always happens: if every little square has an odd number of minus signs, every loop flips the sign an even number of times.
So any two tilings have the same sign. Nothing cancels, and the determinant counts every single tiling.
Now the full chessboard, with the same signs: minus on the vertical edges of every other column. The determinant is twelve million, nine hundred eighty-eight thousand, eight hundred sixteen.
Listing one tiling per second would take five months. The determinant does it in an instant.
And it's not really about chessboards. Squares are vertices, dominoes are edges, and a tiling is a perfect matching.
By 1967, Kasteleyn had made it work for any graph you can draw without crossings. This is the FKT algorithm: it counts the perfect matchings of any planar graph, in polynomial time.
And the story kept going. In 1989, Vijay Vazirani pushed it to graphs with no K three three hiding inside, and Leslie Valiant later built his holographic algorithms on top of it.
When a physicist needs to count twelve million tilings, they don't count. They take a determinant, and then let the board go to infinity.
Let's step back. Ants that never meet. Tilings of a hexagon. Boxes in a corner. Mountain ranges. Aztec diamonds. Chessboards.
All counted by one determinant each.
And it's the same trick every time. Count everything, the families that meet and the ones that don't, each with a sign.
The meeting ones pair up with opposite signs, and cancel. What's left is exactly what you wanted.
For a computer scientist, that's remarkable. Counting is usually hopeless: counting perfect matchings of a general graph is sharp-P complete. That's Valiant, in 1979.
But if your puzzle turns into non-touching paths, or a matching on a planar graph, it becomes one determinant, and polynomial time.

And this isn't only a trick for puzzles. In 1997, Meena Mahajan and V. Vinay computed the determinant itself the same way: write it as a big signed sum, pair up every unwanted term with one of opposite sign, and let them cancel. No division needed.
Determinants can count, because minus signs can cancel.
As for our ants: they can finally go home in peace. Twenty ways home, and they never had to meet.
Thanks for watching.
